title: What types of memory are present in the Java Memory Model (Heap, Stack, Method Area/Metaspace, PC Register, Native Method Stack), and how is each managed?
shortTitle: What types of memory are in the Java Memory Model?

s1_definition.profdef: The JVM runtime divides memory into several areas. The Heap is a shared region where all objects and arrays live and is managed by the garbage collector. Each thread has its own Stack holding method frames with local variables and partial results. The Method Area, implemented as Metaspace since Java 8, holds class metadata, static fields, and the runtime constant pool. Each thread has a PC Register pointing to the current instruction, and a Native Method Stack for native code. Some areas are shared across threads and some are per-thread.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture National Bank of India's building. The Heap is the giant shared vault where all the actual account objects for Rajesh and Priya are stored, and a cleanup crew (the garbage collector) removes boxes nobody references anymore. Each teller (thread) has their own private desk (Stack) where they keep the paperwork for the one transaction they are handling right now, and when they finish a step the paper is cleared off the desk. The Method Area is the rulebook room that stores the blueprints of every form type and the shared static notices. Each teller also has a bookmark (PC Register) showing which line of the procedure they are on, and a side table (Native Method Stack) for when they call an outside specialist.
s1_definition.oneliner: Heap holds objects and is GC-managed and shared; Stack holds per-thread method frames and auto-clears; Method Area/Metaspace holds class metadata; PC Register and Native Method Stack are per-thread bookkeeping.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The JVM runtime divides memory into several areas. The Heap is a shared region where all objects and arrays live and is managed by the garbage collector. Each thread has its own Stack holding method frames with local variables and partial results. The Method Area, implemented as Metaspace since Java 8, holds class metadata, static fields, and the runtime constant pool. Each thread has a PC Register pointing to the current instruction, and a Native Method Stack for native code. Some areas are shared across threads and some are per-thread.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture National Bank of India's building. The Heap is the giant shared vault where all the actual account objects for Rajesh and Priya are stored, and a cleanup crew (the garbage collector) removes boxes nobody references anymore. Each teller (thread) has their own private desk (Stack) where they keep the paperwork for the one transaction they are handling right now, and when they finish a step the paper is cleared off the desk. The Method Area is the rulebook room that stores the blueprints of every form type and the shared static notices. Each teller also has a bookmark (PC Register) showing which line of the procedure they are on, and a side table (Native Method Stack) for when they call an outside specialist.

**One line to remember:** Heap holds objects and is GC-managed and shared; Stack holds per-thread method frames and auto-clears; Method Area/Metaspace holds class metadata; PC Register and Native Method Stack are per-thread bookkeeping.

sections.s2_technical:
The Heap is the largest area and is shared by all threads. Every object you create with new, and every array, lives on the heap. You never free heap memory manually; the garbage collector reclaims objects that are no longer reachable. The heap size is bounded by the flags `-Xms` for the initial size and `-Xmx` for the maximum. For example `new Account("SAV2001", ...)` places the Account object on the heap, and only the reference variable lives elsewhere.

Each thread has its own Stack, created when the thread starts and destroyed when it ends. Every method call pushes a new frame onto the stack holding that method's local variables, parameters, and partial results. When the method returns, its frame is popped, which automatically frees those locals with no garbage collection needed. The stack size is bounded by `-Xss`, and if recursion goes too deep the stack overflows, producing a StackOverflowError. For example a local variable `BigDecimal amount` inside a transfer method lives on that thread's stack.

The Method Area holds per-class information: the class structure, method bytecode, static fields, and the runtime constant pool. Since Java 8 this is implemented as Metaspace, which lives in native memory rather than inside the heap, and grows as needed, bounded by `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize`. This replaced the old fixed-size PermGen and removed a common source of PermGen out-of-memory errors. Static fields like a shared `BANK_NAME` constant are stored here, not per object.

The PC Register is a tiny per-thread area that holds the address of the JVM instruction currently being executed by that thread, so the thread knows where to resume after a context switch. The Native Method Stack is a per-thread stack used when Java code calls native methods through JNI. A senior nuance worth stating is that the term Java Memory Model in the strict sense also refers to the rules about visibility and ordering of reads and writes across threads, governed by happens-before and the volatile and synchronized keywords, but in this question we are describing the runtime data areas, which is the common interview meaning. Keeping both meanings clear shows depth.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India processes transfers on many threads at once. The team needed to understand which data is shared and which is private, because shared data needs care for thread safety while private data does not. This is exactly what the memory areas explain, because Account objects live on the shared heap and can be seen by many threads, while each thread's local variables live on its own stack and cannot be seen by others.

Problem 2 — A constant like the bank name and a running counter of total transfers needed to be shared across the whole application, not copied per object. This is exactly what the Method Area and static fields are for, because static state lives in the class metadata area and is shared by every instance and thread.

In the mini-project we build a transfer that makes each area visible. We define an `Account` whose objects live on the heap, a `TransferService` with a static counter stored in the Method Area and local variables stored on the stack, and a demo that transfers between Rajesh and Priya. We log which values are heap-resident objects, which are stack-resident locals, and which are static class-level state, so the reader can map each piece of data to its memory area.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/mem/MemoryDemo.java

# Run with explicit memory-area flags to make each region visible
#   -Xms/-Xmx = heap, -Xss = per-thread stack, MaxMetaspaceSize = Method Area
java -Xms128m -Xmx256m -Xss512k -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=128m \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.mem.MemoryDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001, 1000000) and Priya (CUR3001, 250000), with a transfer of 50000 from Rajesh to Priya and 10000 from Priya to Rajesh.

Step 1: The main method runs on the main thread. When it executes new Account twice, two Account objects are allocated on the shared heap. The variables rajesh and priya are references that live in the main thread's stack frame and simply point to those heap objects.

Step 2: service.transfer is called for the first transfer. A new stack frame is pushed onto the main thread's stack containing the locals from, to, amount, and before. The object references point at the same heap Account objects, so the method operates on shared heap data through private stack references.

Step 3: Inside transfer the balance check passes, so debit and credit run. These mutate the balance fields inside the heap objects, changing Rajesh to 950000 and Priya to 300000. The static totalTransfers in the Method Area is incremented to 1. When transfer returns, its stack frame is popped and the locals vanish automatically.

Step 4: service.transfer is called again for the second transfer. A fresh stack frame is pushed, the heap objects are mutated again to Priya 290000 and Rajesh 960000, and totalTransfers becomes 2. The frame is popped on return.

Step 5: The demo logs the static BANK_NAME and totalTransfers from the Method Area, and the balances read from the heap objects. The output shows the final heap state and the shared static counter, mapping each value to its area.

```text
[INFO] Transferred Rs.50000 Rajesh → Priya
[INFO] Transferred Rs.10000 Priya → Rajesh
[INFO] Bank: National Bank of India | total transfers (static, Method Area): 2
[INFO] Rajesh (heap object) balance: Rs.960000
[INFO] Priya  (heap object) balance: Rs.290000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Main Thread STACK                         Shared HEAP
  ┌───────────────────────┐                ┌────────────────────────┐
  │ main() frame          │   reference    │ Account(SAV2001,Rajesh)│
  │   rajesh ─────────────┼───────────────▶│   balance (mutated)     │
  │   priya  ─────────────┼───────────────▶│ Account(CUR3001,Priya) │
  │ transfer() frame      │                │   balance (mutated)     │
  │   from,to,amount,before│               └────────────────────────┘
  └───────────────────────┘
          │ frame popped on return (locals auto-freed)

  METHOD AREA / METASPACE          PC REGISTER (per thread)
  ┌───────────────────────┐        points to current bytecode instruction
  │ BANK_NAME (static)    │        NATIVE METHOD STACK (per thread)
  │ totalTransfers (static)│       used for JNI/native calls
  │ class metadata         │
  └───────────────────────┘
  Heap = GC managed/shared; Stack = per-thread auto-free.
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — JVM Memory Layout of a Banking Service Instance ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    JVM Process                            │
  │  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐ │
  │  │  HEAP        │  │ Metaspace    │  │ Per-Thread Areas │ │
  │  │  (shared)    │  │ (native mem) │  │  Stack ×N        │ │
  │  │  Account objs│  │ class meta,  │  │  PC Register ×N  │ │
  │  │  GC managed  │  │ static fields│  │  Native Stack ×N │ │
  │  │  -Xms/-Xmx   │  │ MaxMetaspace │  │  -Xss each       │ │
  │  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └─────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Request threads share heap + metaspace, own their stacks.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Where each value lives ═══

  ── Value placement ──
  new Account(...)        → HEAP (object), ref on STACK
  balance field           → inside the HEAP object
  local 'amount','before' → current STACK frame
  static BANK_NAME        → METHOD AREA / METASPACE
  static totalTransfers   → METHOD AREA / METASPACE
  current instruction ptr → PC REGISTER (per thread)
  JNI call bookkeeping    → NATIVE METHOD STACK (per thread)

  ── Lifecycle ──
  HEAP object: lives until unreachable → GC reclaims
  STACK frame: lives until method returns → popped (no GC)
  METASPACE class: lives until its classloader is GC'd

  Management:
    Heap     → garbage collector, bounded -Xms/-Xmx
    Stack    → automatic push/pop, bounded -Xss (overflow → SOE)
    Metaspace→ native, grows as needed, bounded -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The JVM divides its runtime memory into several areas, and the cleanest way to describe them is by what they hold and whether they are shared or per-thread. The Heap is the large shared region where every object and array lives, so anything I create with new goes there, and it is managed entirely by the garbage collector, bounded by the initial and maximum heap flags. I never free heap memory by hand; the collector reclaims objects once they become unreachable.

Each thread has its own Stack, which holds a frame for every method currently executing on that thread, and each frame stores that method's local variables, parameters, and partial results. When a method returns, its frame is popped and those locals are freed automatically with no garbage collection involved, which is why stack memory is fast and self-cleaning. The stack size is bounded per thread, and if recursion runs too deep the stack overflows and I get a StackOverflowError.

The Method Area, which since Java 8 is implemented as Metaspace in native memory, holds the per-class information: the class structure, method bytecode, the runtime constant pool, and static fields. This is where a shared constant like the bank name and a static counter of total transfers live, one copy for the whole class rather than per object. Metaspace grows as needed and replaced the old fixed-size PermGen, which removed a common out-of-memory problem. On top of these, each thread also has a tiny PC Register holding the address of the instruction it is currently executing, and a Native Method Stack used when Java calls native code through JNI.

In my banking work this mental model matters because it tells me what is shared and therefore needs thread-safety care. Account objects sit on the shared heap and can be seen by many request threads at once, whereas each thread's local variables sit on its own private stack and cannot be seen by others, and static state sits in Metaspace shared by everyone. One senior nuance I always add is that the phrase Java Memory Model also has a stricter meaning about the visibility and ordering of reads and writes across threads, governed by happens-before, volatile, and synchronized, so I clarify which meaning is intended. So my complete answer is that the heap is shared and GC-managed for objects, the stack is per-thread and auto-freed for method frames, the Method Area or Metaspace holds class metadata and statics, and the PC Register and Native Method Stack are small per-thread areas for instruction tracking and native calls.

---

keyPoints: Heap: objects and arrays — shared across threads, managed by GC
Stack: per-thread — local variables, method calls, references
Method Area/Metaspace: class metadata, static fields, constant pool
Program Counter (PC): per-thread, tracks current instruction
Native Method Stack: for native (C/C++) method calls
